text.hook:
A constexpr function with constant arguments
can still run at run time.

The real rules, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Swipe ➜
text.body:
Inside:
1. constexpr vs consteval vs constinit
2. The context decides, not the arguments
3. What the constant evaluator rejects
4. is_constant_evaluated traps and if consteval
5. How constexpr grew, C++11 to C++23
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: When compile-time evaluation is guaranteed, consteval vs constinit, and 6 myths.

slides.title: Eligibility, not speed
rows: **May** run at compile time, in a constant context
**Must**: every call is evaluated at compile time
slides.takeaway: Constant folding at `-O2` is separate: not guaranteed, and it never makes a value usable as a template argument.

slides.title: Is `f()` evaluated at compile time?
slides.takeaway: Parameters are never constant expressions inside the body, even in a compile-time call. Use template parameters.

slides.title: What the evaluator rejects

cards.label: Undefined behaviour
cards.text: Signed overflow, null dereference, division by zero, uninitialized reads: compile error.

cards.label: Escaping allocations
cards.text: `constexpr std::vector<int> v{1, 2};` fails: memory must be freed before evaluation ends.

slides.takeaway: Only for evaluations that really happen at compile time. The same call at run time is ordinary UB.

slides.title: Two traps, one fix
items: `if constexpr (std::is_constant_evaluated())` is **always true**. GCC warns with `-Wall`
`if (std::is_constant_evaluated()) return ce(x);` with a `consteval` `ce` does not compile
The result depends on the call's context, not on `-O0` / `-O2`

slides.title: C++11 to C++23
steps: C++17: constexpr lambdas, `if constexpr`, more of the library (`std::array`, `string_view`)

slides.hero:
Hitting a limit is
a compile error, not
a run-time fallback.
slides.lead: GCC defaults: recursion depth 512, 262144 iterations per loop, 33554432 operations in total.

items.myth: "A `constexpr` function is evaluated at compile time."
items.truth: Only when the context makes it a constant evaluation. Elsewhere it is a normal call.
No run-time version exists, its address cannot escape, every call must be constant.
It means initialized at compile time. The variable stays mutable.

items.myth: "In a compile-time call, my parameter is a constant expression."
items.truth: Parameters never are. Use template parameters.
It is always true. Use plain `if` or C++23 `if consteval`.
Only transient allocations: the vector must die before evaluation ends.

slides.hero:
The context decides.
Not the keyword.
Not the argument.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The same call `sq(10)` five times.
Constant argument, constexpr function.
So all five run at compile time. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: `is_constant_evaluated()` reports which calls really ran in the compiler.

slides.title: What does it print?

bullets: `a`: a `constexpr` variable requires a constant: compile time.
`b`, `c`: plain locals. Run-time calls, even with a constant argument.
`d`: a static is constant-initialized when possible: compile time.
`e`: a `const int` with a constant initializer is constant-evaluated.
slides.wrong: "B: the arguments are constants, so the compiler evaluates it at compile time"

slides.title: Change only the type of `e`
slides.code:
const double f = sq(10);
std::cout << f;    // 100: run time
bullets: A `const double` is never usable in constant expressions, so its initializer is an ordinary call.
slides.takeaway: The context of the call decides compile vs run time, never the arguments alone.

text.hook:
The unit test is a `static_assert`.
The expected sum is correct.
Green build?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Sum the last k elements of an array.

slides.title: Does the test pass?

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11: non-constant condition for static assertion. Subscript '5' is outside the bounds
bullets: The loop condition `i <= 5` reads `a[5]`: one past the end.
During constant evaluation, UB **must** be diagnosed.
The `static_assert` turns the off-by-one into a build failure.
Without the test: run-time UB. One plain GCC 11 `-O0` build printed 681087.
slides.wrong: "B: the test passes, the bug only shows at run time"

slides.title: Stop before the end
slides.tip: This only covers inputs you actually test at compile time. The same call at run time is ordinary UB.
slides.takeaway: `static_assert` tests of constexpr functions are a free UB detector.

Two of them are `const`.
Which ones can size a `std::array`?

text.body: One old rule still decides this.

slides.title: Which declarations compile?

bullets: A `const` **integral** variable with a constant initializer is a constant expression: a C++98 rule.
A `const double` never is, even with a literal initializer.
The cast in (2) does not help: `ratio` itself is not a constant.

slides.title: Say what you mean: constexpr
slides.takeaway: Use `constexpr` for every compile-time constant. The `const int` special case does not extend to other types.

text.hook:
A `static constexpr` limit inside a struct.
Passed to `std::max`.
Same code, C++14 and C++17. Same result?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: No templates, no headers of your own, 10 lines.

slides.title:
Build with `-std=c++14 -O0`,
then `-std=c++17`

slides.verdict: D. C++14 link error, C++17 prints 100
bullets: C++14: the in-class line is only a declaration. No storage exists.
C++17: `static constexpr` members are implicitly `inline`: the declaration is the definition.
C++14 at `-O2` linked here: the value was inlined. Still wrong, just hidden.
slides.wrong: "A: constexpr values have no storage, so they cannot cause link errors"

slides.title: C++17, or define it once
slides.tip: By value (`int m = Limits::MaxQty;`) was always fine. References, addresses and `const T&` parameters are odr-uses.
slides.takeaway: static constexpr members are inline since C++17. Before that, odr-use needs an out-of-class definition.
